The description (3/3) Page 3 of 3 More skills, harder choice Skills that look alike leave the AI guessing; a short list in the project instructions takes the guess away. Hick 1952, Hyman 1953: choice-reaction experiments in people. That a longer list makes an AI choose worse is an inference, not a measured result. Vercel's agent evals: pass rate The skill, by default 53 % + a line in AGENTS.md telling the agent to use its skill 79 % With the line, the skill was opened in 95%+ of cases. One docs skill, one framework. A docs index replacing the skill reached 100%. Name it as an action, lowercase words joined by hyphens Anthropic 's skill-authoring best practices: names use lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only; action-oriented names such as process-pdfs and analyze-spreadsheets are listed as acceptable (the gerund, processing-pdfs , is preferred), and patterns should stay consistent across a collection. collect-sediment-sample film-transect log-dive In the story: Near-twin cards leave the pilot guessing; the list on the wall settles it.

What it costs to load A loaded skill is a recurring token cost. The loaded SKILL.md stays in the context window: a recurring token cost. Which models and agents it works with which robots A skill's value depends on the model and the agent it runs in. Tested in the agent it ships to: the same model in another harness can turn a skill's effect around. When it retires Deprecate it when its evals keep failing or its workflow is retired. Pin production skills to a version; deprecate when evals consistently fail. SKILL.md , its metadata map --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Use when we reach a new site and need a sample … metadata: owner: survey-team version: "1.3" tier: organisation works-with: Claude Code, Codex retire-when: evals keep failing --- The Agent Skills format has no owner field; these keys are a convention. Not settled yet: no common practice so far. In the story: The fleet manual's front page. Fleet, ship and project are the tiers; the robots are the models and agents. Fleet, ship and project are this Episode's words, not vendor terms: vendors tier skills by audience and risk, not by how general the content is. Codex splits repository skill folders from user skill folders the same way Claude Code does.

Sharing it (3/3) Page 3 of 3 Does the skill make things better? Test a skill by running the same task with and without it, because a bad skill can do worse than none. Same task, twice “Take a sediment sample at a new site.” prompt: “Take a sediment sample at a new site.” Without the skill no skill: the baseline skill disabled: the baseline no card no card sediment stirred up Score · illustration 2 / 4 Held 2 m above the seabed Camera checked for loose sediment Core tube sealed Core over 30 cm With the skill the skill loaded collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md loaded 2 m skill · procedure card SKILL.md Score · illustration 3 / 4 Held 2 m above the seabed Camera checked for loose sediment Core tube sealed Core over 30 cm Test the description too Does the AI reach for the skill at the right moment? A few requests each way, near-misses included. The trigger set tests this line of the front matter: --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Takes a sediment core. Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- Should trigger the skill should_trigger: true “ Take a sediment sample at Site 7. ” “ Get a seabed sample here. ” “ New site: sample the sediment. ” Should not trigger the skill should_trigger: false “ Film the seabed at Site 7. ” “ Log yesterday's dive. ” “ Sample the water column here. ” near-miss The agentskills.io guide to descriptions suggests about 20 queries, 8 to 10 each way, each run about 3 times. Did you know? In one benchmark, skills an AI wrote for itself before solving the task, with no good run behind them, scored below having no skill. SkillsBench, 2026: 8.1 to 11.5 points below the no-skill baseline, in all three configurations tested. Of 98 public skills, 92 showed no significant effect; harmful ones lost up to 17.0 points. In the story: Two test dives in shallow water, the same task each time. Not Vercel's result: there, the skill tied no skill.

Writing thirty skills is easy. Owning thirty is the hard part. In the story: A card with a running tag, like a loan statement.

Keeping it alive (2/4) Page 2 of 4 The model changes, the skill doesn't A model update changes who reads your skill, so a skill that worked yesterday can behave differently today. The skill, unchanged collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md same words Collect sediment sample Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- … 2. Descend slowly to the seabed. Model update Your provider ships a new version of the model. The skill keeps the same words, and the same instruction now gives a different result. The same collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md , a new model version reading it. collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md unchanged model new version today: stops short yesterday Different model or agent A colleague runs your skill in another app or agent, even on the same model, and it reads the same words its own way. The same collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md , run in Claude Code and in Codex: another agent, even on the same model. collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md unchanged agent, model another one today: into the silt yesterday Did you know? Lehman's laws Software in use must keep being adapted, or it becomes progressively less satisfactory. Here the skill stays put and the world around it moves. Disputed: of the laws, only continuing change and continuing growth held in every study reviewed. Same words, a new reader Anthropic's prompting guide has model-specific sections on where "a single model behaves differently"; OpenAI notes that prompts optimized for other models "may not immediately work". Your SKILL.md is read as text by whichever model runs it. Anthropic's guide shows "what to change in your prompt" per model; OpenAI: prompts optimized for other models "may not immediately work". In the story: Same card, two dives, two depths. Analogy only: the pilot keeps his piloting and forgets the days. A skill file is read as text, closer to a written note than to a trained skill.

A thought experiment No speaker notes for this Slide.

An AI model that forgets every morning Each AI conversation starts fresh: Mollick's forgetful coworker Ethan Mollick advises treating AI "like an infinitely patient new coworker who forgets everything you tell them each new conversation" 1 . Claude Code sessions each begin "with a fresh context window" and only written files carry knowledge across 2 . "Amnesiac" is the Episode's word, not Mollick's. Sources (2) Ethan Mollick, Getting started with AI: Good enough prompting, One Useful Thing (24 Nov 2024) ( opens in a new tab ) oneusefulthing.org Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com

A skill hands the AI your procedure A skill spares you the repeat Anthropic contrasts skills with prompts: a skill spares you from repeating the same guidance across conversations 1 . When a request matches a skill's description, Claude reads SKILL.md and only then does that content enter the context 1 . Calling a skill by name loads it too, as the Slide on two ways to call a skill shows. Sources (1) Anthropic, Agent Skills overview ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com
What a skill is No speaker notes for this Slide.
When to write one No speaker notes for this Slide.

The third time is the signal When to write a skill: Fowler's rule of three "The first time you do something, you just do it. The second time you do something similar, you wince at the duplication, but you do the duplication thing anyway. The third time you do something similar, you refactor." 1 It is a heuristic, not a measured result. The credit to Don Roberts is in the 1999 book, which the research could not read. Sources (1) Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code (1997 slides) ( opens in a new tab ) pdfs.semanticscholar.org The model as a new employee: why the rule of thumb holds Anthropic tells the writer to think of Claude as "a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows", and to show a prompt to a colleague with minimal context 1 . Anthropic Engineering calls building a skill "like putting together an onboarding guide for a new hire" 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Prompting best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Anthropic Engineering, Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Where the model is not like a person each is backed by a source, but listing them as the breaks is a synthesis: sessions start fresh, so only written files carry over 1 ; rules in a file are "context, not enforced configuration" 1 ; newer models read instructions more literally 2 ; the same words read differently by model 2 ; assistants drift toward agreeing with the user 3 . Sources (3) Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com OpenAI, GPT-4.1 Prompting Guide ( opens in a new tab ) developers.openai.com Sharma et al., Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Not every repeat deserves a skill Skills written too early: Knuth on premature optimisation "We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%" 1 . His reason is a cost, and the same paper calls ignoring efficiency in the small "an overreaction", so it is a rule about timing and measurement. The quotes were not checked against the original (the ACM page returned 403). Sources (1) Knuth, Structured Programming with go to Statements ( opens in a new tab ) dl.acm.org Skills nobody needs yet: YAGNI, and what it does not cover "Always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you need them" 1 . Fowler counts four costs of a presumptive feature (build, delay, carry, repair) and says YAGNI does not apply to effort to make software easier to modify 2 . Sources (2) Jeffries, You're NOT gonna need it! ( opens in a new tab ) ronjeffries.com Fowler, Yagni ( opens in a new tab ) martinfowler.com A crowded skill index costs the AI too by default every skill's description is loaded on every turn, unless the skill is user-only, and Claude Code and Codex cap or shorten the skill listing, so a crowded index can shorten or drop descriptions 1 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com OpenAI, Build skills (Codex docs) ( opens in a new tab ) learn.chatgpt.com

Write it from a good run Write the skill from a real run the standard advises: "Complete a real task in conversation with an agent, providing context, corrections, and preferences along the way. Then extract the reusable pattern into a skill." A skill an LLM writes from general knowledge alone yields "vague, generic procedures" 1 . Sources (1) Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io The agent can interview you Anthropic's skill-creator checks the current conversation for a workflow the user wants to capture, extracts answers from it first, then interviews the user to fill gaps 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, skill-creator SKILL.md ( opens in a new tab ) github.com Run the task without a skill first: Google's route Day 3 suggests asking your most experienced practitioner to "narrate three workflows they do regularly", picking the most repeated one, running the prompts without any skill loaded, and drafting a SKILL.md from the transcript. It closes with "Resist the urge to let an LLM generate fifty skills on day one." 1 This agrees with the standard's advice to extract from a real run. It is Google's vendor guidance, not a measured result. Sources (1) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com
The description No speaker notes for this Slide.

The description is the trigger Description carries the whole burden because only name and description load at startup, "the description carries the entire burden of triggering. If the description doesn't convey when the skill is useful, the agent won't know to reach for it" 1 . Sources (1) Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Descriptions and information scent Pirolli and Card's abstract names "information scent models, which address the identification of information value from proximal cues" 1 . It is a finding about people foraging for information; that a vague label gives a model less to go on is an inference, not their finding. The page-646 definition was read second-hand. Sources (1) Pirolli and Card, Information Foraging (Psychological Review, 1999) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org

Name the trigger, not the content A description says what and when the standard says a description "Should describe both what the skill does and when to use it" and include keywords that help agents identify relevant tasks 1 . Anthropic adds specific triggers and contexts, because Claude chooses among potentially 100+ skills by it 2 . Sources (2) Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Write the description in the user's words "Use imperative phrasing", "Focus on user intent, not implementation", and "Err on the side of being pushy. Explicitly list contexts where the skill applies" 1 . Sources (1) Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io "Not for" lines in a description: Google's advice alone the standard and Anthropic recommend no "not for" clause in a description. Over-triggering is handled there by testing near-miss queries that share keywords but need something different, which "test whether the description is precise, not just broad" 1 . Sources (1) Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io The "not for" clause in Google's Day 3 Google's Day 3 whitepaper writes "explicitly state what it is not for", gives the example "Do NOT use for employee shift scheduling or financial accounting", and its checklist says "Include when NOT to use to prevent over-triggering" 1 . It calls the description "your routing algorithm. It is the only thing the model sees to decide whether to load the Agent Skill" and asks to "be pushy if the model under-triggers". It gives no measurement that the clause helps, so it is Google's vendor guidance, a choice between sources. Sources (1) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com

More skills, harder choice Choosing among many skills: Hick and Hyman, a finding about people Hick applied information theory to choice-reaction-time experiments with up to ten alternatives 1 . Hyman reports that reaction time rises linearly with the amount of information in the choice 2 . That a longer list makes an AI choose worse is an inference, not a measured result. Sources (2) Hick, On the Rate of Gain of Information (Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1952) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Hyman, Stimulus Information as a Determinant of Reaction Time (Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1953) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org An AGENTS.md index beat skills: Vercel's test a line in AGENTS.md telling the agent to use its skill raised the pass rate from 53% to 79%, and the skill was opened in 95% or more of cases 1 . A compressed docs index of about 8KB in AGENTS.md, replacing the skill, reached 100%. Vercel's working theory: no decision point, and skills load only when invoked 1 . It is one docs skill for one framework, not a procedure. Sources (1) Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals ( opens in a new tab ) vercel.com Skills too broad or too narrow the standard warns that skills "scoped too broadly become hard to activate precisely", while too narrow forces several to load 1 . No source measures lookalike skills lowering the pick rate directly. Sources (1) Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Name each skill as an action Anthropic's skill-authoring best practices say a skill's name uses lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only, prefer the gerund form (processing-pdfs) and list action-oriented names such as process-pdfs and analyze-spreadsheets as an acceptable alternative; they advise against inconsistent patterns within a skill collection 1 . This Episode names its skills in the action form, collect-sediment-sample. Sources (1) Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices (Claude Platform docs) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com
What context goes inside No speaker notes for this Slide.

What context goes where Information architecture, as Nielsen Norman Group defines it "Information architecture is the practice of structuring and organizing content on your site." 1 The Slide shows this sentence verbatim, with the source named; the site is read as the skill and its project by analogy. Sources (1) Tankala, Information Architecture vs. Sitemaps, Nielsen Norman Group (3 Sep 2023) ( opens in a new tab ) nngroup.com Information architecture, in its authors' words "a design discipline that is focused on making information findable and understandable" 1 ; one of their four definitions is "The structural design of shared information environments" 2 . "The craft of organising information so it can be found" is a paraphrase, not their wording. Sources (2) Rosenfeld, Morville and Arango, Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond, 4th ed., Part I introduction ( opens in a new tab ) oreilly.com Rosenfeld, Morville and Arango, Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond, 4th ed., ch. 2 ( opens in a new tab ) oreilly.com Every line of a loaded skill is a recurring token cost Once loaded, a skill's content "stays in context across turns, so every line is a recurring token cost" 1 , and every token "competes for the agent's attention" 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io

A project detail couples a skill to one project Coupling, as first written "The fewer and simpler the connections between modules, the easier it is to understand each module without reference to other modules" 1 . It is a design principle for code modules, applied to skills by analogy. Sources (1) Stevens, Myers and Constantine, Structured design ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Project details hard-coded into a skill can override the task In a benchmark of 98 public skills, a generic workflow template made the agent write files to .github/workflows/ when the task required ci/; the authors advise abstract guidance over templates with hard-coded paths 1 . It is one worked example, not a test of this picture. Sources (1) Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Inside the skill Move detail out of SKILL.md, and say when to read it "Keep your main SKILL.md under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material to separate files" 1 . The key is telling the agent when to load each file, for example "Read references/api-errors.md if the API returns a non-200 status code" 2 . Sources (2) Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Long reference files start with a contents list "For reference files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top. This ensures Claude can see the full scope of available information even when previewing with partial reads" 1 . This is Anthropic's account of Claude's behaviour and no source measures its effect. Sources (1) Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com References stay one level deep Claude "might partially read files when they're referenced from other referenced files", using commands such as head -100, so references stay one level deep from SKILL.md 1 . The standard states the rule without the reason 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Progressive disclosure, as Anthropic names it Anthropic's docs say the filesystem-based design "allows progressive disclosure: Claude loads information in stages as needed, rather than consuming context upfront" 1 . Supporting files opened only at the step that needs them are the same idea as the three loading levels. Sources (1) Anthropic, Agent Skills (Claude Platform docs) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com
What context stays beside No speaker notes for this Slide.

Beside the skill A skill teaches the class of problem and reads the instance a skill "should teach the agent how to approach a class of problems, not what to produce for a specific instance"; the example reads the schema from references/schema.yaml instead of writing joins into the skill 1 . Claude Code offers ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} so a skill can reference project files independent of where it is installed 2 . Sources (2) Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com

Who uses it, and where Where a skill is stored encodes who gets it Claude Code skills in the home directory load "in every project", skills committed to a repository reach "everyone who works there", and plugins or managed settings reach "a whole team" 1 . Codex splits repository folders from user folders the same way 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com OpenAI, Build skills (Codex documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) learn.chatgpt.com The skill scope matrix is an inference no published framework combines the two axes into a 2x2 with care levels; the nearest are one-axis tier schemes 1 . Microsoft's zoned governance ties care to audience for agents, not skills: private personal agents, approved environments and admin approval for shared ones 2 . Label the square a rule of thumb. Sources (2) Saha and Hemanth, Skilldex: A Package Manager and Registry for Agent Skill Packages with Hierarchical Scope-Based Distribution ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Microsoft, Implement a zoned governance strategy (Copilot Studio) ( opens in a new tab ) learn.microsoft.com Evals matter once a skill is shared 40 of 98 skills change sign between two harnesses running the same model, so a skill is best evaluated "with the model, agent, and repositories in which it will be deployed" 1 . Sources (1) Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

grill-with-docs keeps context beside the skill Project context written beside the skill, read next run Anthropic says models, like people who use "file systems, inboxes, and bookmarks", do well with notes kept outside the context window 1 , and a skill should teach an approach while reading instance details from files 2 . The grill-with-docs files are this repository's own copy of Matt Pocock's skill 3 , not a research source. The Slide shows grill-with-docs only; the grill-me skill is not shown. Sources (3) Anthropic Engineering, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Pocock, skills (GitHub repository; skills/engineering/grill-with-docs) ( opens in a new tab ) github.com
Sharing it No speaker notes for this Slide.

Shared skills are knowledge articles A skill registry entry Anthropic's enterprise guidance says to keep a registry entry per skill with purpose, owner ("Team or individual responsible for maintenance"), version, dependencies and evaluation status including the last evaluation date 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com A skill review date is an adaptation Knowledge-Centered Service does not review on a schedule: "Let reuse of Not Validated articles be the review" 1 , and the page does not use the word "owner". Owner, version and a calendar review date combine KCS and Anthropic's guidance; no source defines them as a rule for skills. Sources (1) Consortium for Service Innovation, KCS v6 Practices Guide, Technique 5.2: KCS Article State ( opens in a new tab ) library.serviceinnovation.org The Agent Skills format has no owner field the Agent Skills format has no owner, version or review-date field; its optional metadata map holds them by convention 1 . Anthropic also says "Skill authors should not be their own reviewers" 2 . Sources (2) Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

Who owns the shared skill library Shared skills are tiered by audience Anthropic's tiers in claude.ai: personal skills, skills shared with individuals, group skills bundled in a plugin, and organisation-wide skills that only owners can add or remove 1 . "Fleet, ship, project" are the Episode's words, not vendor terms; vendors tier by audience and risk, not by how general the content is. Sources (1) Anthropic, Provision and manage skills for your organization ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com Who adds, reviews and removes shared skills the org library offers "Requires review", "Open" and "Off", a reviewer approves "a fixed version" and users stay on it until a new one is approved 1 . Anthropic says to pin production skills to a version and to deprecate skills whose evaluations consistently fail or whose workflow is retired 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Provision and manage skills for your organization ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Token cost and model fit are per-skill facts a loaded skill is a recurring token cost 1 , and a skill's value depends on the model and harness it runs in 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Skill governance "still being worked out" is a judgement Anthropic's enterprise guidance lists what to track per skill (purpose, owner, version, evaluation status) and does not report how many organisations do so 1 , so the unsettled corner is the Episode's judgement, not a measured claim. Sources (1) Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

Does the skill make things better? Skills that score below no skill: SkillsBench, not Vercel skills written by the agent itself land 8.1 to 11.5 points below the no-skill baseline on all three configurations tested 1 . In Vercel's eval the skill tied the baseline at 53%; only sub-scores dipped (lint 89% against 95%, test 58% against 63%) 2 . Do not attribute "below no skill" to Vercel's headline. Sources (2) Li et al., SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals ( opens in a new tab ) vercel.com Bad skills can hurt, many do nothing of 98 public skills, 92 showed no statistically significant effect, and harmful ones lost up to 17.0 points by anchoring the agent on their own templates 1 . Curated skills raised the average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% 2 . Sources (2) Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Li et al., SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Test the skill's description too the trigger set in the agentskills.io guide to descriptions is "about 20 queries: 8-10 that should trigger and 8-10 that shouldn't", each run about 3 times 1 . Anthropic's guide says to build scenarios and compare against a no-skill baseline 2 . "Three and three" is in neither. Sources (2) Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Trigger tests in Google's Day 3: two sizes Day 3 says a description must pass checks "to hit the industry-standard 90% trigger accuracy rate", the first being "You must write 3 positive and 3 negative triggers", with no source for the rate. Elsewhere it says "Write three eval cases (two positive, one negative) before drafting the body" 1 . Its own counts disagree, it is Google's vendor guidance, and none of it is measured. Sources (1) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Skill evals in Google's Day 3: one figure misread Day 3 says "a skill stripped of its instructions scored 58%, while the agent without the skill scored 63%" 1 . In Vercel's post that is the default skill against the baseline on the test sub-score alone, and overall they tied at 53% 2 . Vercel's wording wins, and SkillsBench in the first note, not Day 3, is the evidence for skills scoring below no skill. Sources (2) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals ( opens in a new tab ) vercel.com
Keeping it alive No speaker notes for this Slide.

Every skill is a loan Skill upkeep as technical debt: Cunningham's words "Shipping first time code is like going into debt. A little debt speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with a rewrite." "Every minute spent on not-quite-right code counts as interest on that debt." 1 He names the failure mode as "the failure to consolidate". The software parallel to skills is an inference, not his claim. Sources (1) Cunningham, The WyCash Portfolio Management System ( opens in a new tab ) c2.com

The model changes, the skill doesn't Skills in a changing world: Lehman's first two laws, and their limits "E-type systems must be continually adapted else they become progressively less satisfactory"; complexity increases "unless work is done to maintain or reduce it" 1 . The laws are disputed: only continuing change and continuing growth were validated by all studies reviewed 2 , and Linux grew super-linearly 3 . Sources (3) Lehman, Ramil and Wernick, Metrics and Laws of Software Evolution: The Nineties View ( opens in a new tab ) users.ece.utexas.edu Herraiz, Rodriguez, Robles and Gonzalez-Barahona, The evolution of the laws of software evolution: a discussion based on a systematic literature review ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Godfrey and Tu, Evolution in Open Source Software: A Case Study ( opens in a new tab ) plg2.cs.uwaterloo.ca Each model reads the same instructions differently Anthropic's guide has model-specific sections on where "a single model behaves differently and what to change in your prompt" 1 ; OpenAI notes that prompts optimized for other models "may not immediately work" 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Prompting best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com OpenAI, GPT-4.1 Prompting Guide ( opens in a new tab ) developers.openai.com The model's memory and patient H.M.: an analogy that breaks at the skill H.M. learned mirror drawing and kept it across 3 days while remembering none of the sessions 1 , because skills are stored by a memory system outside the damaged region 2 . For a model this maps only as analogy: trained weights fit the skill side, but a skill file is read as text, which makes it closer to a declarative note. That mapping is inference; Milner 1962 was read only through Squire's account. Sources (2) Squire, The Legacy of Patient H.M. for Neuroscience ( opens in a new tab ) pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Squire, Conscious and Unconscious Memory Systems ( opens in a new tab ) pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov The agent changes the skill too, even on the same model in a benchmark of 98 public skills, 40 change sign between two harnesses running the same model, and the authors advise evaluating a skill "with the model, agent, and repositories in which it will be deployed" 1 . Sources (1) Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Retire skills Retire a skill: archive over delete Knowledge-Centered Service prefers archiving to deleting, because deleting can break links and an archived article can be restored 1 . Anthropic says to deprecate a skill whose evaluations consistently fail or whose workflow is retired 2 . Reading the dive log to pick what to archive is the Episode's own method. Sources (2) Consortium for Service Innovation, KCS v6 Practices Guide, Technique 5.2: KCS Article State ( opens in a new tab ) library.serviceinnovation.org Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

The whole iceberg Skill governance: what is settled, and what is not no source defines owner and review date as a rule for skills, and none shows how many organisations govern shared skills at all 1 . The audience-by-scope matrix is a rule of thumb, not a published framework 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Skills for enterprise ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Saha and Hemanth, Skilldex: A Package Manager and Registry for Agent Skill Packages with Hierarchical Scope-Based Distribution ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:31 You are the captain Imagine you work with an AI model that is brilliant at its job, the most capable colleague you have. I will give it a picture, because we need one all the way down: you are the captain of a coastal research project, and the model is your pilot of ten years, who steers a diving robot on a cable from the control room on deck while you decide where the project goes next. 0:31 – 0:53 One settled condition Your pilot has one condition, and it never changes. He forms no new memories overnight, but he keeps everything he ever learnt as a pilot, every rule of the trade. That is an AI model: what it learnt in training stays, and what you told it in yesterday's conversation is gone.

An AI model that forgets every morning 0:00 – 0:31 Three mornings So the next morning you open a new conversation, and the model knows nothing of yesterday. In our picture the pilot greets you with "Nice to meet you", you explain how to take the sediment sample step by step, and the robot waits on deck while you talk. The morning after, it is the same greeting and the same explanation, and by the third morning you could recite it in your sleep. 0:31 – 0:45 The hook That is what working with AI feels like today, because every conversation starts from zero on how you work. You've explained this to the AI a hundred times. It has heard it once. 0:45 – 1:09 What would you do So here is my question, and I would like your honest answer: if you worked with this model for a whole season, what would you do about it? If you're with me in a workshop, type it into the chat now. If you're watching the recording, pause here and answer out loud. I'll come back to it.

A skill hands the AI your procedure 0:00 – 0:32 The answer Most people land on the same idea within a minute: write it down. Write the procedure once, keep it where the model can find it, and let the model read it when the task comes up, instead of you explaining it again every morning. That is a skill, and in our picture it is a procedure card in the dive manual at the console. The rest of this Episode is about doing it well. 0:32 – 0:58 Three things to remember Hold on to three terms, because we return to them all the way down. The skill is the procedure itself, the card. Its description is the one line that tells the model what the skill is for, an entry in the manual's index. And the project instructions hold what is true for this one project, the project brief on the wall. 0:58 – 1:21 The card slides out And here is the part that matters most: the model does not read every skill you have. It reads the descriptions, and it opens one skill when the task needs it, the way one card comes out of the manual when the dive needs it. (pause) That is the picture for everything that follows.

What a skill is 0:00 – 0:23 Surface first We are still at the surface, so before we ask when to write a skill, let's see what a skill is made of. I'll use the words your chat app uses, and if you work with a coding agent, some Slides have a second view that shows you the files behind each part. 0:23 – 0:39 The mechanics, plainly I want to be exact about how a skill gets loaded, because everything later depends on it. So I say first what the AI really does, and use the dive only to make it easier to picture.

When to write one 0:00 – 0:14 Sunlight We are one level down, in the sunlit zone. Here we decide two things: when a task deserves a skill at all, and how to describe it so the model actually picks it. 0:14 – 0:31 Borrowed principles From here on I borrow principles from engineering, information architecture and UX, and they all lean on one idea: what works for people also works for AI. I say that as a strong rule of thumb, not as a law. 0:31 – 0:52 Why a rule of thumb It holds because the model acts only on what you hand it, like a capable newcomer on their first day. It is only a rule of thumb because there are places where it breaks, and I've put those in the notes on the next Slide for you to read.

The third time is the signal 0:00 – 0:27 Three tries So when does a task become a skill? Think about what you learn each time you explain it to the model. The first time you find out what is needed at all, the second time you tighten it, and by the third time you can tell what a good result looks like, which is the moment you know what you would be writing down. 0:27 – 0:42 Not only repetition But counting is not enough. If you cannot check whether the result was good, you are not capturing a procedure, you are copying a habit, and the skill will repeat your habit with great confidence. 0:42 – 1:03 Did you know Software engineers arrived at this the same way, long before any AI tool: they call it the rule of three, from Fowler's Refactoring, a rule against generalising too early. I'll leave the exact wording in the notes, because the point here is only that people got there first.

Not every repeat deserves a skill 0:00 – 0:13 Too early Now the opposite danger. If you write the skill after the first run, you freeze a guess, and a procedure nobody has proven now carries the authority of a skill. 0:13 – 0:33 A thin card has a price And every quick skill has a price. It is one more thing to keep right and one more line in an index that only grows, so picture a manual stuffed with thin cards, several of them never tested, until the one you need is buried in the middle. 0:33 – 0:54 Three questions So before you write a skill, ask three questions. Does the task repeat, does it have rules, and does a mistake cost something? If the answer is no to all three, leave it in the chat. This check is mine, a practical filter I use, not a published test.

Write it from a good run 0:00 – 0:21 Two starting points Say it is the third time and you are ready to write the skill. There are two good places to start: your own notes from earlier runs, the logbook pages of earlier dives, or a run with the AI that has just gone well, today's dive, while it is fresh. 0:21 – 0:43 Capture the why With the fresh run, ask the AI to interview you before it writes anything: why that depth, why that order, what would have counted as failure. You want the skill to hold your intent and not only the steps, because steps without the why break the first time the situation changes. 0:43 – 1:15 While he still knows Then let it write the skill in the same conversation, while the whole run is still in its context window. Tomorrow it will have forgotten, and that is the condition we started with. So that is your first step: pick one task you've explained three times, and turn a good run of it into a skill. In a coding agent, that is one sentence: ask it to turn this conversation into a skill.

The description 0:00 – 0:12 The label decides We are still in sunlight, and this is the part most people skip. A skill the model never picks helps nobody, so the description matters more than the instructions. 0:12 – 0:26 Name, description Before the model opens a skill, it sees two lines: the name and the description. That is all the index holds, and it is all the model has to decide with.

The description is the trigger 0:00 – 0:29 The pilot's view Sit in the model's chair for a second. At the start of a task it has every skill's name and description in front of it, and none of the instructions behind them, like a pilot with the index open and every card closed. So unless you call the skill by name, the description is the trigger: it decides whether the model picks the skill on its own. 0:29 – 0:43 Two entries Take two descriptions for the same skill: "Samples", and "Take a sediment sample at a new site". A task comes in, because we have just reached a new site. Which one would you open? 0:43 – 1:09 Scent Researchers who study how people search call this information scent: the cue on a label that tells you whether it leads where you want to go. They found it in people, and I am lending it to the model. So your job is to make the description smell like the task it serves, because that scent is what pulls the trigger.

Name the trigger, not the content 0:00 – 0:34 Two labels Here are two descriptions for the same skill. The first names the content, "SOP-07: corer handling, steps 1 to 9", and the second says what the skill does and names the moment, "Takes a sediment core. Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed". One says only what is inside, the other names the trigger, when you need it, and that is your second step: write the description as the moment you'd need it. 0:34 – 0:58 Your request Now it is the day of the dive and you type, "Grab some mud here before we move on." Nothing in "SOP-07, steps 1 to 9" tells the model when it is needed, but "a sample from the seabed" does, so only the moment description matches. Write it in the words you would actually say. 0:58 – 1:21 The closing line Last, the moment description can end on a second half: "Not for water samples or filming." It tells the model where the skill stops, so it does not open it for a job it cannot do. Treat that half as a choice and not a rule, and test whether it helps your skill.

More skills, harder choice 0:00 – 0:16 Near-twins Now see what happens when the skills pile up. "Sample", "Take sample", "Seabed sample v2": three skills whose descriptions sound alike, and a model that has to guess between them. It guesses, and you made it do so. 0:16 – 0:40 A short list on the wall The fix is cheap: a short list in your project instructions, AGENTS.md if you work with a coding agent, that says "In this project, use these three skills." Project instructions are always loaded, so the model no longer has to choose from a crowded index. On our ship, that is a list on the wall. 0:40 – 1:06 Hick's law People have the same trouble: the more the options look alike, the longer it takes to choose, and psychologists call that Hick's law. I am lending it to the model, so hold it as a picture, not a measurement. What I want you to take from this Slide is the short list: it is short, and it is always loaded. 1:06 – 1:31 Name it as an action One more habit keeps the index tidy: name each skill as an action, in lowercase words joined by hyphens, like collect-sediment-sample. A name that says what the skill does tells the model, and you, what it is for before anyone reads the description, and when every name follows the same pattern, a near-twin stands out before it gets written.

What context goes inside 0:00 – 0:13 Twilight Deeper now, into the twilight zone, where the light is dim. The skill is written and described, and the question is what context goes into it and what stays beside it. 0:13 – 0:28 A decision, not a law I want to be careful with the word rule here. Keeping the procedure apart from project details is a design decision with trade-offs on both sides, so I'll show you the trade-offs and you decide.

What context goes where 0:00 – 0:28 A home for each fact Take one piece of project knowledge, something that changes from one project to the next, like the depth of today's dive site. It needs a home, and you have to pick one. Choosing where each piece of context lives is information architecture, the same craft that decides where things go on a well-built website, and you practise it whether or not you call it that. 0:28 – 0:47 Three costs Every home costs you in three ways. Performance asks whether the model actually reads it at the moment it needs it, reusability asks how many projects the skill still fits, and token cost asks how much of the context window it fills, and how often. 0:47 – 1:26 Three homes There are three homes for it. Inside the skill, it arrives every time the skill runs, but now the skill fits only this project. In your project instructions, it sits in the context window on every task, whether the task needs it or not, and the skill stays free for any project. In a project file the skill reads, it is loaded only at the step that needs it, and the skill fits every project. None is right in general, so it depends on how many projects the skill will serve.

A project detail couples a skill to one project 0:00 – 0:23 Scribbled in Take a sampling skill with one project detail written into it: "descend to 40 metres", true at site 4. At site 7 the seabed lies at 120, and the robot hangs uselessly at 40 while the model follows the skill perfectly. (pause) The skill was followed to the letter, and the dive still failed. 0:23 – 0:41 Coupling Engineers have a word for this mistake: coupling. The 40 metres written into the skill ties it to one place. For a skill it comes down to this: keep project details out, so the skill has no ties to one project.

Inside the skill 0:00 – 0:24 Extras by step So what can safely live inside a skill? Domain knowledge, kept in supporting files and tied to the step that needs it. Step three, lower the arm, runs a script, the arm preset. Step four, identify what you collected, reads a reference file, the species guide, and step six, label the sample, fills in a template. 0:24 – 0:39 The long step When one step's instructions grow long, move the next paragraph into a reference file and leave a pointer in the step, so the instructions stay short enough for the model to take in at once. 0:39 – 0:54 Contents first And start every long reference file with a contents list, because the model may only skim the top. When step four opens the species guide, its contents page alone tells the model what else is inside.

What context stays beside 0:00 – 0:15 Beside, not inside Now the other home: project details that stay outside the skill, in project files it reads when it runs. The procedure goes inside, and whatever changes from one project to the next stays beside. 0:15 – 0:29 Where it gets shared And who uses the skill decides how much care it needs. A skill for your own use can be loose, and a skill a colleague runs needs more, which sets up the next Section.

Beside the skill 0:00 – 0:21 The card points Here is the mistake from before, fixed. The skill no longer says 40 metres. Its step says "descend to the depth in today's dive plan", and that dive plan is a project file the skill reads when the step runs: site 4, 40 metres, site 7, 120 metres. 0:21 – 0:41 Same card, any site Replay site 7. It is the same skill with no edit, and this time the robot reaches the seabed at 120 metres. The procedure stayed put and the site details lived in the project file, which is your third step in miniature: decide where the project details live. 0:41 – 0:58 For developers In the coding-agent view the step names a project file, say CONTEXT.md, and the agent reads it when that step runs. For everyone else, it is any document in your project that the skill tells the model to read.

Who uses it, and where 0:00 – 0:12 Two questions Here is a decision tool, and it asks two questions. Who uses the skill, only you or others too? And where, in any project or in one in particular? 0:12 – 0:48 Four squares Four squares come out of that. Personal and project-specific: write the details straight in, it needs the least upkeep. Personal and general: keep the details beside, it is your own toolkit. Shared and project-specific: the details can live in its supporting files, and the project team owns it. Shared and general: the details sit beside, with an owner, a version and evals. So as a skill moves from your own notebook into the shared library, it loses its project details and gains an owner. 0:48 – 1:02 A rule of thumb This matrix is a rule of thumb, and the label is mine. It is how I think about it, so try it on your own skills and tell me where it breaks.

grill-with-docs keeps context beside the skill 0:00 – 0:18 The interview is the card Let me show you inside and beside together, on real files instead of the dive. This is grill-with-docs, a skill by Matt Pocock that I use, and it runs an interview, which is the procedure. It stays the same every time. 0:18 – 0:33 Follow the arrow While it runs, grill-with-docs writes files beside itself, a glossary and decision records, and the next run checks your words against them. The skill stays the same, and what it learned about your project waits beside it. 0:33 – 0:47 Skills can run skills One last thing: a skill can also run other skills: grill-with-docs runs one called grilling and another called domain-modeling. There is no settled name for that yet, and I'll leave it there.

Sharing it 0:00 – 0:10 Midnight Now we are in deep water, the midnight zone. Everything so far was for you, so what changes when a colleague runs your skill? 0:10 – 0:22 Three jobs Three jobs wait down here. Give the skill an owner and a version, decide who looks after the shared library, and test that the skill actually helps.

Shared skills are knowledge articles 0:00 – 0:18 Your notebook A personal skill has no header at all, like a card in your own notebook. That is fine while it is only yours, because you know who wrote it, when you last used it, and who fixes it when it breaks. 0:18 – 0:42 Into the fleet manual Once you share it into your team's skill library, the fleet manual on our ship, it needs what any company knowledge article has: an owner, a version, and a date for its next review. It is the same skill with a control block on top, and your personal skills can skip this until you share them. 0:42 – 1:03 Why Why bother? Because once it is shared, one author's edit changes what the model does for everyone who runs it, and nobody knows whom to ask when it goes wrong. That is your third step: before you share a skill, decide where the project details live, and give it an owner.

Who owns the shared skill library 0:00 – 0:12 Back to the square Come back to the matrix, to the shared, general square. That is the kind of skill the most people rely on, so it is where care matters most. 0:12 – 0:36 What the front page needs A shared library needs rules beyond the owner and the version: who may add a skill, which tier it sits in and so whom it reaches, what it costs to load, which models and agents it works with, and when it retires. Each is a question somebody has to answer before the skill goes in. 0:36 – 0:55 The dark corner And then there are the questions nobody has settled yet. I want to be plain with you: I do not have the answers there, and I don't think many organisations do yet. If you have worked it out in yours, I would like to hear how.

Does the skill make things better? 0:00 – 0:21 Same task twice How do you know a skill helps? Run the same task twice, once without the skill and once with it, and compare the results, like two test dives in shallow water. Don't trust your feeling about it, because feeling useful and being useful are not the same thing. 0:21 – 0:37 The callout (pause) And this test matters more than it sounds, because a skill is not automatically a gain. A bad skill can leave the model worse off than no skill at all, which is the whole reason the comparison exists. 0:37 – 0:57 Test the label Test the description too. Take a few requests that should trigger the skill and a few that should not, and include near-misses, the ones that sound like the skill but need something else. Those show you whether the model reaches for it at the right moment.

Keeping it alive 0:00 – 0:09 The Abyss This is the deepest zone, the abyss, months later. Writing the skill was quick, and keeping it right is the work. 0:09 – 0:20 Nobody sees it Most people stop at the first good run, and the part below it gets little attention, which is why I want to spend three Slides here.

Every skill is a loan 0:00 – 0:07 Quick to write A skill takes five minutes to write. That is the loan: you get the speed now. 0:07 – 0:27 A running tab Then the statements arrive, one line at a time. The project details changed, a new tool arrived, and a description now overlaps another skill's. None of them is a disaster, and each is a small cost that piles up. Engineers call it technical debt, Ward Cunningham's phrase. 0:27 – 0:39 Owning thirty Writing thirty skills is easy. Owning thirty is the hard part, because the cost was never in writing the skill, it is in keeping it right, month after month.

The model changes, the skill doesn't 0:00 – 0:24 Not the only pilot There is one more thing that changes under your skill, and you do not control it: the model that reads it. Every AI model has the condition we started with, and each AI provider trains its own, the way each pilot school trains its own pilots. So the reader of your skill is never fixed. 0:24 – 0:59 Update and switch Two things can change the reader. A model update: your provider ships a new version, your skill keeps the same words, but an instruction like "descend slowly" now gives a different dive. A different model or agent: a colleague runs your skill in another app, and it reads the same words its own way. The skill did not change, the reader did, and engineers saw this long ago in software: what is in use has to keep changing, or it gets worse. 0:59 – 1:13 Hand over the verdict So here is my question to you: which of your skills would you re-check after the next model update? If you own one, would you trust it to behave the same way tomorrow?

Retire skills 0:00 – 0:14 Read the log Last job: retire skills. Put your list of skills next to what your work actually used this season, the dive log on our ship, and see which skills no task ever opened. 0:14 – 0:25 The archive box Those skills go into an archive, each with the date it was retired, so the decision is written down and nobody wonders later where a skill went. 0:25 – 0:43 Short index again And the index left behind is short again, with the one you need easy to find. Remember the description buried in the middle of a stuffed manual a few Slides ago? It is back in view, and the model can pick it.

The whole iceberg 0:00 – 0:24 Three steps Let me bring the three steps up from the seabed. One: pick a task you have explained three times, and turn a good run of it into a skill. Two: write its description as the moment you would need it. Three: before you share it, decide where the project details live, and give it an owner. 0:24 – 0:39 The honest caveat I want to be honest about the deep end. Governance, review and retirement are the part I am least sure about, and I am still learning there too. If you find something that works, tell me. 0:39 – 0:54 Your first card We are back on deck, with a short index. If you want a low-key start, take the task you explained last week and turn its best run into your first skill. Thank you.
